lead: A vapour compression refrigerator is a Rankine plant turned around: it spends work to move heat from a cold room to a warmer place. The compressor raises the pressure of a refrigerant vapour, the condenser rejects heat, a throttle drops the pressure, and the evaporator takes heat in at a low temperature. The same loop cools homes, shops, cold storages and car cabins. Its performance is read from refrigerant property tables or a p-h chart, because the expansion valve is isenthalpic and every term in the COP is an enthalpy difference.
prereq: You need: the Rankine cycle for the four-component loop, and Unit 5 for reading property tables and charts.

sections.h3: The loop and its four parts

blocks.text: A refrigerator takes heat Q<sub>L</sub> from a cold space at temperature T<sub>L</sub> and rejects heat Q<sub>H</sub> to a warm space at T<sub>H</sub>. The second law says this cannot happen without work input. In a vapour compression cycle the work is put in by a compressor, and the refrigerant changes between liquid and vapour as it moves around the loop.

Four steady-flow components make the loop. The evaporator is a heat exchanger where low-pressure liquid refrigerant boils at TL and absorbs QL. The compressor takes vapour from state 1 and raises it to state 2, so its pressure and temperature rise. The condenser rejects QH to air or water at TH, and the vapour condenses to liquid at state 3. The expansion valve is a throttle: it drops the pressure from state 3 to state 4 without work, and the refrigerant enters the evaporator as a low-pressure liquid-vapour mixture.

The standard state numbers are fixed: 1 is compressor inlet, 2 is compressor outlet, 3 is condenser outlet, and 4 is expansion-valve outlet. The compressor handles vapour, not a two-phase mixture, which is why the cycle is called vapour compression. A pump cavitates on a vapour-liquid mixture, so the loop is built so that the compressor takes dry vapour. Liquid carried over into the compressor damages it, which is why a little suction superheat is always provided.
Treat each component as steady flow and neglect kinetic and potential energy changes. The throttle is isenthalpic, so h<sub>4</sub> = h<sub>3</sub>.
q<sub>L</sub> = h<sub>1</sub> − h<sub>4</sub>,  w<sub>c</sub> = h<sub>2</sub> − h<sub>1</sub>,  q<sub>H</sub> = h<sub>2</sub> − h<sub>3</sub>
blocks.where: q<sub>L</sub> is the refrigeration effect in kJ/kg; q<sub>H</sub> is the heat rejected in kJ/kg; w<sub>c</sub> is compressor work in kJ/kg; h is specific enthalpy in kJ/kg, with states 1 to 4 as in the figure.
COP<sub>R</sub> is the coefficient of performance of the refrigerator, dimensionless.
T<sub>L</sub> is the cold-space absolute temperature in K; T<sub>H</sub> is the warm-space absolute temperature in K. This is the upper bound between the same two temperatures.

blocks.text: For a required cooling duty Q̇<sub>L</sub> in kW, the mass flow is ṁ = Q̇<sub>L</sub> / q<sub>L</sub>, in kg/s. One tonne of refrigeration is 3.5 kW.

items: Raising evaporator pressure raises T<sub>L</sub> and raises COP.
Lowering condenser pressure lowers T<sub>H</sub> and raises COP.
Suction superheat protects the compressor from liquid droplets but costs COP.
Liquid subcooling before the throttle increases the refrigeration effect and gains COP.

sections.h3: p-h and T-s, and where the losses come from

blocks.text: On a pressure-enthalpy (p-h) diagram, the saturation dome is the boundary between liquid-vapour mixture and single phase. Compression 1→2 runs up and to the right. Condensation 2→3 is a horizontal line at condenser pressure. The throttle 3→4 is a vertical line because enthalpy is constant. Evaporation 4→1 is a horizontal line at evaporator pressure. The horizontal distance 1→4 is the refrigeration effect, and 1→2 is the work.

On a temperature-entropy (T-s) diagram, ideal compression 1→2 is vertical if it is isentropic. After isentropic compression, state 2 lies in the superheated region, so 2→3 first desuperheats outside the dome and then condenses as a horizontal line inside the dome at condenser temperature. The throttle 3→4 is not vertical: it falls in pressure and entropy rises, so the line curves down and to the right inside the dome. Evaporation 4→1 is at constant temperature and pressure. A common mistake is to draw 3→4 as an isentropic drop.

A real cycle falls below the Carnot COP because throttling is irreversible, because suction vapour is superheated to protect the compressor, because pressure drops occur in pipes and heat exchangers, and because the compressor is not perfectly isentropic. These are the same kind of irreversibilities that keep a real Rankine plant below its ideal efficiency.

Common refrigerants include R-134a for domestic refrigerators and car air conditioning, R-410A for split air conditioners, ammonia for cold storage and food plants, and carbon dioxide for heat pumps and transcritical systems.

examples.question: A vapour compression refrigerator using R-134a works between an evaporating temperature of −10 °C and a condensing temperature of 40 °C. The property data give h<sub>1</sub> = 395.0 kJ/kg, h<sub>2</sub> = 435.0 kJ/kg, and h<sub>3</sub> = 250.0 kJ/kg. Find the refrigeration effect, the compressor work, the COP, the Carnot COP between the same temperatures, and the mass flow for one tonne of refrigeration.
steps: The expansion valve is isenthalpic, so h<sub>4</sub> = h<sub>3</sub> = 250.0 kJ/kg.
Refrigeration effect: q<sub>L</sub> = h<sub>1</sub> − h<sub>4</sub> = 395.0 − 250.0 = 145.0 kJ/kg.
Compressor work: w<sub>c</sub> = h<sub>2</sub> − h<sub>1</sub> = 435.0 − 395.0 = 40.0 kJ/kg.
Absolute temperatures: T<sub>L</sub> = 273.15 − 10 = 263.15 K; T<sub>H</sub> = 273.15 + 40 = 313.15 K.
One tonne of refrigeration is 3.5 kW. Mass flow: ṁ = 3.5 / 145.0 = 0.0241 kg/s.
examples.answer: The refrigeration effect is 145.0 kJ/kg, the compressor work is 40.0 kJ/kg, COP is 3.625, Carnot COP is 5.263, and the mass flow for one tonne is 0.0241 kg/s.
examples.check:
h1 = 395.0
h2 = 435.0
h3 = 250.0
h4 = h3
qL = h1 - h4
wc = h2 - h1
cop = qL / wc
TL = 273.15 - 10
TH = 273.15 + 40
carnot = TL / (TH - TL)
duty = 3.5
mdot = duty / qL
print(f'{qL:.1f}')
print(f'{wc:.1f}')
print(f'{cop:.3f}')
print(f'{carnot:.3f}')
print(f'{mdot:.4f}')

traps: Drawing the expansion 3→4 as isentropic on the T-s diagram. The throttle is isenthalpic, not isentropic; entropy rises and the line curves inside the dome.
Using the condenser heat h<sub>2</sub> − h<sub>3</sub> as work input. The only work input is the compressor work h<sub>2</sub> − h<sub>1</sub>; the throttle gives no shaft work at all.
Putting heat rejected in the COP numerator. COP<sub>R</sub> = q<sub>L</sub>/w<sub>c</sub>, using the cooling effect, not q<sub>H</sub>.
Using °C in the Carnot formula. T<sub>L</sub> and T<sub>H</sub> must be in kelvin.
Forgetting that one tonne of refrigeration is 3.5 kW, or mixing kW with kJ/kg so that the mass flow unit comes out wrong.

quiz.q: Name the four components of a vapour compression refrigerator in the order of refrigerant flow.
Why is the expansion valve treated as isenthalpic?
quiz.a: It is a throttle with no shaft work and negligible heat transfer, so the steady-flow energy equation gives h<sub>3</sub> = h<sub>4</sub>.

quiz.q: A cycle has h<sub>1</sub> = 400 kJ/kg, h<sub>2</sub> = 450 kJ/kg, and h<sub>3</sub> = 240 kJ/kg. Find the refrigeration effect and COP.
A refrigerator has a duty of 5 tonne and a refrigeration effect of 120 kJ/kg. Find the mass flow.
What happens to COP when the evaporator pressure is raised, with the condenser pressure fixed?
quiz.a: T<sub>L</sub> rises, the compressor pressure ratio falls, and the work per kg falls. COP generally rises, though the refrigeration effect may change slightly.

quiz.q: Give two reasons why a real vapour compression cycle has a lower COP than the Carnot value between the same temperatures.
quiz.a: Throttling is irreversible, and suction superheat plus pressure drops and non-isentropic compression add losses.

quiz.q: What does one tonne of refrigeration mean in kW?
quiz.a: One tonne of refrigeration is 3.5 kW of cooling.

beyond: Not for the exam. Inverter air conditioners vary compressor speed instead of switching on and off, so the cycle moves between points rather than sitting at one design point. CO<sub>2</sub> systems can run transcritical, above the critical pressure, where the condenser becomes a gas cooler. Ejector and cascade cycles are used to recover expansion work or reach very low temperatures. Refrigerant selection now balances performance with environmental rules. Search next for variable-speed vapour compression, transcritical CO<sub>2</sub> refrigeration, and ejector refrigeration cycles.
